title: Passkeys
tagline: A passkey signs you in without a password to steal or a code to read out. Why can't it be phished, and where is the weak spot that's left?

client.name: User
client.brief: The person signing in. Confirms with a touch, a fingerprint or a PIN.

application.name: Browser
application.brief: Carries requests between the website and the authenticator, and states where a page really came from.

idp.name: Authenticator
idp.brief: The phone or security key. Holds one private key per website and never lets it out.

mcp.name: Website
mcp.brief: Holds only public keys. Issues a fresh challenge and checks the signature that comes back.

teaches: A passkey is a key pair made for one website. The private key never leaves the authenticator; the website stores only the public key.
The browser, not the page, says which site is asking. A look-alike site has no key to ask for.
Every sign-in signs a fresh challenge, so a recorded response is worthless later.
The remaining weak spot is the way back in when the passkey is lost.

glossary.means: A key pair created for one website, used instead of a password.
The real address a page was loaded from, as the browser sees it.
A random value the website sends for one sign-in attempt. The authenticator signs it.
The authenticator checking it is really you (fingerprint, face, PIN), not just that someone touched it.
The website that relies on the passkey to know who you are.
A number some authenticators raise with each use. If it ever goes backwards, a copy exists.
